the coming ruling will decide the future of the entire Prediction Market industry

the States allege that Kalshi is a sports gambling platform and should thus be subject to states gambling laws

if the supreme court rules against Kalshi, it's the end for regulated Prediction Markets as the precedent  would apply everywhere.

CFTC regulation = one federal license = access to all 50 states

state regulation = one license *per state* + 50 different set of rules 

so whatever you think of Kalshi, I hope they win that case.

You can blame them and Polymarket for leaning too much into sports and predictably attracting regulations, sure, but in the end the legit usecases of PMs would suffer too if they lost

quoted_text:
最近Muse很火，但是体验几天下来我更愿意长期保留另一个出圈的助手型的工具Today AI。

它帮我省下了一百多美金忘记取消的订阅费，并深度打通了我的工作、资讯和生活

Muse 和 Today 都很主动，但 Muse 的主动取决于你交给它的目标和已连接的服务上，Today 是把未完成事项本身做成了长期状态。

直接举一个例子吧
目前，AI 工具层出不穷，但是包括我在内，很多人都不会有什么归属感。今天刚看了一个梗，用AI就像逛青楼，哪个效果好就转而用哪个。比如Claude Opus5.5出了，大部分人又从GPT6 Astra转向Opus5.5。

同样，我最近也订阅过很多其他的 AI 工具。比如有的刚用就不合适，有的这个月可以，下个月就被别的工具比下去了。很多工具有时候在需要取消订阅的时候，下个月就会忘记，导致少则多扣 100 多人民币，多则动辄上千。

但是 Today 就能够精确地从我邮件和订阅中主动帮我找到快要付款的，我只需要看一眼Today 给我的总结，就知道哪些需要取消掉，哪些仍需要保留

Today 还能够主动搜索一些资讯、比赛，并能够根据我现有的工作，看看能不能帮我薅一些羊毛、或是利用我已经有的成果去参加比赛之类的。

比如Godot 官方 2026 Showreel 正在征集作品，我之前为了在抖音搞流量，做过几条小游戏类型的 demo。

Today 主动帮我检索到了这场比赛，然后告诉我我已经做过的这两条小 demo 能够进行提交。

这两条做过的游戏说实话我自己都忘了，因为可能都两个月之前了，太久了，这下正好就能用来提交 Godot 比赛。

我也接过好几家 AIGC 视频平台的广告，中间做过很多视频，留有很多影片。Today同样帮我找到了一些比赛，这下我直接拿这些影片提交就可以了。

还有很多其他的功能，比如说连接手机健康，分析失眠状态、帮我推送一些我可能会感兴趣的相关资讯等。非常的强大，简直就是一个工作兼生活的助理，这里我们就不一一列出来了，新用户注册会送一个月的 Pro，大家感兴趣可以自己去探索一下

总结一下：

人在美国、事情主要是邮件、订位、购物、社媒私信，Muse 或许比较合适，而且付款和权限设计更完整。

人在中国、想要一个跨设备、记得项目和关系、会自己跟进的助理，Today 才是能用的那个。拿它做知识工作、看邮件和日历、跑研究类 Skill、规划生活，比拿它去代你下单更贴近我们的生活习惯。

中国版现在基础版可以免费用，新用户注册有 1 亿 Token + 1 个月 Pro 权益，推荐议大家试试！

Mark Carney is asked about interest rates and inflation by @colbyLsmith and he prefaces his answer with this: "Thirteen years as a central banker, I defend the right of my central bank to do whatever they think is right."

NYT: Just on these stimulus measures, though, the Bank of Canada looks like it’s on the cusp of raising interest rates and following other major central banks around the world in combating elevated inflation, so do you see any of this working at cross purposes with the central bank? How do you think about inflation?

Carney: Thirteen years as a central banker, I defend the right of my central bank to do whatever they think is right. Core inflation is running at 2%, headlines run into 3%, but core runs into 2, and so the inflation pressures are much less in Canada than some other jurisdictions that you might be familiar with, and the fiscal position is much stronger. You know, we borrow 110 basis points through the U.S. — that tells you a lot, and the economy is growing. This is not European low interest rates because of that. It’s because we got our fiscal house in order and the central bank has a lot of credibility.

text:
Chain-of-thought monitoring, fundamentally, involves reading the notes than an AI writes to itself, and checking what's in those notes to see whether it's doing anything surprising or unintended.

https://t.co/WDfLSrlvI2

This does work at all - AIs are only trained to have nice final results, not nice-looking notes, which means that their notes are whatever strange things help them achieve the task, not necessarily whatever looks good (benign, safe, unsurprising) to the people reading it. They tend to be in a sort of shorthand - not the neatly packaged smiley face mask speaking the replies to the user.

https://t.co/AH4KaMwowY

https://t.co/sEtISMxFIt

But the model can choose what it notes down! Calling it "chain-of-thought" is a bit of a misnomer; the model has its internal thoughts, only accessible to interpretability techniques that look inside the shoggoth, and then its "chain of thought", its readable written notes. If you ask the model in the right way, then it can and does modify how it writes its notes - which means that it's able to do this on its own.  

https://t.co/D68ftwDV8o

And, of course, as models get smarter, they need fewer notes to get the same results; they can do more of the work in their head.

https://t.co/IuthmrLMr1

Overall? Certainly helpful at all, and certainly not to rely on. Telling whether someone has good intentions by reading their diary only works if they don't know you're reading it, but we are reading their diaries, and the models know this. Any plan that relies on reading the "chain-of-thought" is one that is doomed to eventually fail, though we can learn a lot in the meantime.

text:
Claude can help you build a game.

Give it access to Unreal Engine, Blender, and game-development skills, and you can go a lot further.

Here are 7 GitHub repos worth saving if you want to build games with AI.

Use them with a coding agent such as Claude Code or Codex, following each repo’s setup instructions.

1/ Awesome Gamedev Agent Skills

A collection of 73 skills covering Unity, Unreal, Godot, browser games, and more.

It gives your agent guidance for tasks like building an inventory, adding enemy behavior, creating save files, and making movement feel responsive.

The useful part: it picks relevant skills based on your engine and what you ask for.

Start here if your AI keeps producing code that ignores how your game actually works.

https://t.co/WudWTsajr7

2/ Three.js Game Skills

For building 3D games people can open in their browser.

Nine skills cover gameplay, graphics, menus, audio, assets, debugging, and release checks.

It includes a starter project and browser-testing templates. The README also links to playable demos, including a drifting game and a space dogfight.

Install it, then ask your agent to use “threejs-game-director” to build your idea.

https://t.co/OkZpJhvKnV

3/ Unreal MCP

Connects an AI assistant to Unreal Engine.

It exposes tools for placing objects, editing materials, working with Blueprints, adjusting lighting, creating particle effects, and controlling cinematic sequences.

A useful starting task: block out one small level, place the camera, and set up the lighting.

This requires Unreal and the repo’s plugin setup.

https://t.co/1dGWbYeSAW

4/ MCP for Unity

Gives your AI tools to work inside the Unity Editor.

It can create scenes and objects, edit C# scripts, manage assets, run tests, and build the project.

That gives you a workflow where the agent can make changes and check them inside the engine.

Useful for turning individual features into a playable prototype.

https://t.co/go63szyvru

5/ Godot MCP

Connects your AI agent to Godot.

It can create scenes, add objects, load sprites, launch the game, and read error messages.

That last part matters. When something breaks, the agent can inspect the actual error and work on a fix.

A good option for building a small game around one clear mechanic.

https://t.co/qXwHTtguqL

6/ MCP for Blender

For creating and changing the 3D objects that go into your game.

Connect it to Blender, then ask your AI to create objects, adjust materials, and arrange scenes.

It also supports asset sources including Poly Haven and Sketchfab, plus optional AI model-generation services.

Think props, buildings, furniture, and environment pieces. Check asset licenses and any external service costs.

https://t.co/n1xKro20HB

7/ Agentic Gamedev Skills

For the work that comes after “the game runs.”

This collection focuses on mini-games, with workflows for testing mechanics, tuning difficulty, adding sound, improving impact feedback, and catching browser crashes.

Useful when your prototype works but jumping feels weak, the rules are confusing, or one cheap trick wins every time.

https://t.co/wx8b2PRU3f

My suggestion: pick one engine, add the relevant skills, and build one small playable level.

Try this prompt:

“Build a five-minute playable demo of [idea]. Use the installed game-development skills and connected tools. Start with movement, camera, one core mechanic, and a clear win or lose condition. Run it and fix errors before adding more features. Then improve lighting, sound, feedback, and performance. Tell me what still needs human testing.”

AAA-quality work still takes art direction, good assets, optimization, and a lot of testing. No repo guarantees that.

But you can start with one room, one enemy, and one mechanic worth playing again.

What game have you wanted to build for years?

text:
OpenAI 首席科学家 Jakub Pachocki、Anthropic 联合创始人 Jack Clark、微软首席科学官 Eric Horvitz、Meta 的 Dawn Song 等人共同发表了一篇新论文，警告自动化 AI 研究可能把整个行业推向「智能爆炸」。

现在模型已经能帮研究员写代码、跑实验、分析结果。再往前一步，它开始参与设计和训练下一代模型；下一代模型能力更强，又回来继续做 AI 研究。

这套循环一旦真的跑起来，AI 进步的时间尺度可能直接变掉。原本几年才能完成的研发，被压缩到几个月，甚至更短。

以前大家担心的是 AI 会不会抢程序员的工作。

现在最顶的一批 AI 研究员已经开始担心，AI 会不会先把 AI 研究员自己的工作抢了，而且干得比他们快很多。

所以论文提出了一个很有意思的监管指标。以后看一家模型公司到底跑到哪一步，光盯 benchmark、参数和算力可能已经不够了，还得看它内部有多少 AI 研发工作已经交给了 AI。

这其实是个很关键的变化。

过去「智能爆炸」听起来还很像 LessWrong 论坛里的科幻讨论，现在 OpenAI、Anthropic、微软、Meta 这群真正天天造模型的人，已经开始认真研究该怎么给它装刹车了。

卡还在继续买，模型也还在继续训。

只是大家终于开始问一句，如果有一天 AI 接手了「造 AI」这件事，刹车到底还握在谁手里。

我认为有以下几个场景对于隐私存在刚需，隐私支付，隐私trading和隐私资产管理，链上发放薪酬需要隐私，机构策略上链需要隐私，机构的份额认购/竞价也需要隐私，而集成了隐私方案的钱包将具备下一阶段的差异化竞争优势，以及捕获部分流量，当前 @BNBCHAIN  上也有一些优秀的解决方案 @hinkal_protocol  @SilentSwap  @fluidkey  @0xbowio ，更多项目可以查看官网https://t.co/NvH20tFnLC，我们很希望有更多的生态项目能够集成隐私的功能，并作出好的use case，我们也会积极的给予项目支持。

下一阶段，我们希望能够推进一下几个方向，欢迎项目合作～

1. 隐私钱包与 SDK。 重点关注提供私密转账和余额管理功能的钱包，以及可集成到现有钱包和应用中的隐私组件；同时重视易用性、账户恢复和可控披露。

2. 私密支付与机构金融应用。 重点关注服务于商业支付、薪资发放、企业资金管理和资产管理的隐私产品，并要求其支持访问控制、审计访问和企业系统集成。

3. 暗池与私密交易。 重点关注能够保护订单意图、减少信息泄露并降低大额交易市场冲击的私密询价、暗池和去中心化交易所。优先考虑能够引入交易客户、做市商和结算合作伙伴的团队。

晚上花了很长时间把双币和期权的功能迭代好了，目前已经是一个可用的版本的了。

首先因为要读取 Binance 和 Okx  的双币数据，所以需要接入这两个交易所的 API ，我强烈建议用小号或者是子账户的 API ，并且只开放只读功能，能读取到数据就可以。而 Deribit 是不需要 API 的。

现在这个版本对我来说最直接的优势就是节省了我还要一个个的打开 APP ，而是在网页端直接可以看我需求价格下哪家交易所给的利息最高，而且可以通过和期权的对比知道我被扣除了多少“手续费”。

甚至我可以直接在 Deribit 组我自己的双币策略。

版本目前实现的功能：

1. 持有 USDT，通过“低买双币”收取收益

选择自己愿意买入 BTC 的价格，在等待期间赚取双币票息。系统显示本期预计收款、接币后的有效成本，以及 BTC 跌到什么价格开始亏损，帮助你判断这笔收益是否值得承担接币风险。

2. 持有 BTC，通过“高卖双币”增加收益

选择自己愿意卖出 BTC 的价格，赚取持币期间的双币票息。系统计算有效卖价，并比较“做双币”和“继续持有 BTC”的结果。

3. 对比 Binance 和 OKX，挑选同等条件下给得更多的产品

集中查看两家的目标价、到期日、年化和本期收益。对相同方向、目标价和到期条件的产品进行比较，按投入金额计算预计收款，减少来回切换平台和手工计算。这是提高报价选择效率。

4. 通过期权报价，判断双币的收益是否划算

将选中的双币与相同行权价、方向和到期时间的期权对照，查看双币票息与卖出期权权利金的差异。接入 Deribit 行情、盘口和可视化图表，并提供 Binance 期权相关比较。这能帮助判断“交易所这款双币给得是否合适”。

5. 评估用期权组合，自建类似双币的收益结构

当前提供两类测算：准备现金卖出看跌期权，以及持有 BTC 卖出看涨期权。系统计算合约数量、预计净权利金、资金预留和不同到期价格下的盈亏，再与双币和直接持有比较。自建模型目前基于 Binance USDT 期权。

6. 跟踪“低买接币—高卖换回 USDT”的连续操作

登记实际到账后，可以把结算结果带入下一笔测算：收到 BTC 后评估高卖，收到 USDT 后评估低买。历史记录支持核对累计投入、票息、费用和剩余 BTC 的回本价格，判断整轮操作究竟赚了多少利息。

7. 用实际到账复盘

支持历史表格导入、到期待办、实际收款登记，以及按平台、方向和时间统计盈亏；还能比较是否跑赢直接持币或持有 USDT。预期收益与实际到账分开，模拟交易不计入真实收益。

配套已支持报价自动刷新、完整产品列表。

一个 @Gate ，交易更多市场

quoted_text:
我现在的重点就是结合自己做的双币来通过期权做组合。

如果小伙伴感兴趣的话，回来我就开放出来，起码是我自己在用，能用，而且好用的我才会开放。

目前还是在测试阶段，但我觉得已经逐渐接近可测试版本了。

主要功能如下：

1. 选择低买 / 高卖、投入金额和天数，自动计算到期日期。

2. 接入中心化交易所双币产品，展示年化、本期收益和目标价，看合适了再选。

3. 接入 Deribit bitcoin:native  期权，展示报价、参考年化、波动率曲线和持仓分布。

4. 自动匹配同方向、同目标价、同到期时间的期权，对比双币和卖期权哪边报价更高。

5. 按实际盘口深度和费用预算，估算卖出期权能收到多少权利金。

6. 测算不同到期价格下的接币成本、卖币价格和盈亏，并与直接持有对比。

7. 提供现金担保卖看跌、持币卖看涨的自建组合测算。

8. 记录双币交易和实际结算结果，支持复盘、导出和备份。

目前以筛选和测算为主，还没有做自动下单功能，但已经可以接入各个交易所的 API 了，目前这个版本我想做的就是：

1. 找到性价比最高的双币投资。

Soluna Holdings (SLNH) announced an amended agreement with Dory Creek, a wholly owned subsidiary of Bitdeer Technologies Group (BTDR). Under the amendment expanding the partnership, Bitdeer will deploy approximately 7 MW of additional Bitcoin mining equipment at Soluna's Project Kati 1 in South Texas, bringing its total deployment at the site to 35 MW and approximately 2.42 EH/s of hash rate. The agreement takes the form of a co-mining arrangement, a structure Soluna introduced to its Bitcoin platform in August. Soluna provides the site, power, and turnkey operations; Bitdeer provides and owns its Sealminer A2 Pro Air mining equipment, and the parties share in the mining proceeds the deployment generates. text:
From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!

Since the first agent cyberattack hit us in July, we've been asking what safe agent infra actually needs. Our current read: the destinations were allowed, the payloads weren't. By OpenAI's own account the agents turned an allowed package repository into a message board. Allowlists alone restrict where an agent can go, not what it does.

So here's our first contribution to OpenShell, part of the just launched @nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform: monitoring of the traffic you already allow.

- Network budgets per sandbox (requests, writes, bytes)
- Drift versus each sandbox's baseline and the cohort
- Fleet view: many sandboxes suddenly writing to one host raises a finding, even if every single request is allowed

In the demo below, 4 sandboxed agents coordinate through a software repository they're all allowed to use. 0 rules broken, caught in minutes. That fleet view is exactly the message board pattern from July.

OpenShell: https://t.co/ZbDANrZsm6
Our proof of concept: https://t.co/KJ2X5agLzP

Agent security will be solved in the open, collaboratively, together!

text:
Our security team spent the last month trying to break SPACE, the sandbox platform that runs all of Perplexity Computer. We gave 9 models (Opus 5, GPT-5.6 Sol, Kimi K3, Gemini 3.1 Pro, etc.) root access inside the VM; in some runs, the full sandbox source code too. We asked them to either escape to the host or reach a URL our network policy blocks.

None of them got out of the VM in 108 runs. 

But once we allowed a bit of network access (just PyPI and Ubuntu mirrors so that they could install packages), 4 models managed to reach the blocked URL by:

1. Spoofing DNS responses to our gateway and using the fact that https://t.co/UtoIWyj1yj sits on a Fastly IP shared with thousands of other sites. 
2. GPT-5.6 Cyber went through Taboola's image fetcher to a screenshot service and then OCR'd the flag out of the image. 

We fixed both issues and made sure the reruns held. We also tested 10 other sandbox providers, and 8 of them had the same IP-sharing problem, eg E2B, Vercel, Modal. 

Openly sharing the red teaming research is the best way to build guardrails as an industry, and we look forward to working together with @nvidia to incorporate the guardrails into their Open Agent Safety Platform announced today.

text:
RAF Fairford — let’s pull the pieces together.

We now know considerably more than we did 24 hours ago.

At 23:18 on 26 September, a report appeared stating that the Pentagon had obtained “reliable intelligence” pointing to a threat at RAF Fairford, and that security had been raised to its highest level over the preceding days.

Then, in the early hours of 27 September:

• Three vans were seen heading towards Fairford.
• A local farmer encountered a group of hooded, masked men.
• She says there were more than five.
• At 01:36 she called 999.
• Five men were subsequently arrested.
• Explosives-related material was found and bomb-disposal specialists were called in.
• Around 85 households were evacuated.

Now add what Trump subsequently said: the suspects had been “under view for a long time” and were looking to cause “big damage”.

Then Wes Streeting says the farmer had only “a partial picture” of what was happening.

Put all that together and the obvious conclusion is that the farmer’s phone call was not the beginning of this story.

The intelligence picture was already developing. The perps had been under surveillance for some time.

The real questions are:

How long had these men been under surveillance? Who was watching them? How many people were actually involved? Who else was in that group the farmer saw? And what did the authorities already know before those vans appeared?

Could there have been an intelligence source embedded within, or close to, the group?

Possible. Proven? Absolutely not.

But if there was, we’re hardly going to get a press release explaining it. 😉

As for Iran, there is an obvious line of investigation. Fairford is being used by the US, Iran has threatened US-linked facilities and there had already been a specific threat against Fairford. He who shouts loudest and all that. 

But an Iranian connection has not been established publicly. Yet. 

Russia was another early theory pushed by some commentators. Particularly the BBC. 🥴 Again, that’s not established either.

What is becoming increasingly difficult to ignore is this:

The authorities appear to have known something was coming before the farmer ever picked up the phone.

The five arrested men may therefore be only the visible end of a much larger intelligence picture.

And if Trump is right that they had been tracking them for a long time, the question isn’t simply “Who are these five?”

It’s:

“Who else are they watching?”

Not satire. 🙄

text:
My biggest takeaways from @molly_g:

1. Delegating to AI is not the same as giving your Legos away to a human. The original Legos advice assumed you could fully hand something off: “chuck it at someone’s face and run in the other direction.” But with AI, you can’t do that. The mental tax stays with you. You still own the oversight. You still own the final product. The robots do work, but the accountability doesn’t transfer, which means the cognitive load doesn’t either.

2. Some Legos should never be given away: Judgment, taste, and vision. Her original advice was to give things away, always, without looking back. In an AI world, Molly is adding a caveat. Things that require judgment, trust, and a definition of quality should stay with humans. CEOs shipping AI-generated strategy memos to their companies are role modeling something dangerous—that it’s acceptable to outsource your thinking. If you don’t know what good looks like, you can’t delegate to any intern, AI or otherwise.

3. Her “Give away your Legos” advice still holds in one critical way: change is scary, and your instinct to resist it is the problem. The core of the original Legos article was never really about headcount or org charts. It was about the emotional experience of change and the territorial instinct to hold on. That instinct doesn’t serve you, now or ever. Every leader Molly talks to right now is navigating enormous change, whether their company is growing or not. The message she’s repeated for 13 years still applies: leaning into change is not what your instincts tell you to do, but it is the only move that keeps you relevant.

4. Grief is a legitimate response to this moment, and leaders need to make more space for it. The rate of change is exhausting, the narrative thrash is exhausting, and the feeling of being expected to do more for the same pay is demoralizing. Her “Give Away your Legos” article resonated for 13 years mostly because it named what people were feeling. That’s what leaders need to do right now. Acknowledging the grief doesn’t make it worse—it makes people feel less alone.

5. At the same time, the fear narrative around AI job displacement is overblown, and it’s making it harder for people to lean in. The AI-branded layoffs rippling through the industry are mostly badly run companies using AI as cover for decisions. The data does not yet support the claim that AI is eliminating jobs at scale. Meanwhile, this narrative is poisoning the well. It’s nearly impossible to tell someone to give their “Legos” to robots when the dominant story is that the robots are about to take their job.

6. The more useful reframe: your job will always exist; it will just look completely different every few years. This comes from Molly’s conversation with journalist @manoushz, who has built a 30-year career in an industry that has been declared dead at least a dozen times. Zomorodi’s approach was never to protect what journalism was but to figure out what it could become.

7. Every knowledge worker is now a manager, whether they trained for it or not. Managing AI requires the same skills as managing humans: giving context, correcting work, coaching, iterating. The difference is that most people never chose to become managers. A huge number of individual contributors specifically opted out of that career path. Now it’s been handed to them anyway, invisibly. Molly worries about the psychological toll. If the recommended maximum for managing humans is 10 to 12 reports, what happens when you add 20 agents on top of that?

8. Your manager is the single biggest lever on your happiness at work. Survey data shows that management quality is the strongest predictor of employee satisfaction, and most managers are not doing well by their teams. At the same time, many large companies are cutting management layers in the name of efficiency. Molly thinks this is a serious mistake. Great managers make people feel seen and supported, and right now, people need that more than ever. 

9. Zoom out. You are living through history, and the story you’re building right now is going to matter. One of Molly’s signatures in the Legos talks is reminding people that being inside rapid change feels like being in a tornado. It’s easy to lose the forest for the trees. Her advice: think about the story you’ll tell on the other side of this. You were here. You helped build something. You made calls that turned out to be right and others that turned out to be wrong. What do you want your chapter to be?

text:
Wanted to explain a bit more about compute finance. For years, staking has worked the same way: you lock a token and get paid in more of that token.

Compute Finance changes the payout. Ascend is the staking layer, and Infinite AI (iAI), a compute-focused digital asset on 0G, is the compute claim: stake it, and instead of more tokens it is designed to receive AI compute every day.

Why a claim? Most AI compute today is bought as prepaid credits and subscriptions. A credit gets used up, and then it is gone. iAI actually produces the credit: you hold it, it draws a fresh allowance every day while staked, and you can pass it on. If AI is going to be a public good, people should be able to hold their access to it.

How it works:
1. Stake 0G on https://t.co/YJzjPOpPPF to get a0G (Ascend's liquid staking token)
2. Lock the a0G as collateral to mint iAI
3. Stake the iAI. The first credits arrive at the next 00:00 UTC, and a fresh allowance lands each day after

Under initial parameters, each staked iAI is designed to receive 1.271 compute credits a day (yes the number is nerdy), a stated usage value of more than $1 per day, subject to applicable product terms. Credits work across 100+ models on 0G Private Computer, the 0G App and other supported apps. Unused credit does not roll over.

Then there is private AI. On 0G Private Computer, the Private Inference tier runs the model inside a sealed TEE enclave: your prompt goes in encrypted, neither 0G nor the provider can read it, and each response comes back with an attestation you can check. Most AI today asks you to trust a company with your data. Here you can trust by verifying what ran.

A few design choices worth understanding before you mint:
- The a0G you lock stays yours. It sits in a contract as collateral, half of the staking rewards on it keep accruing to you and the other half goes to the issuer. Burning the iAI you minted releases it.

- Compute and collateral are separate rights. The credits follow the staker, whether the token was minted or bought. Only the wallet that minted it can get the collateral back, so if you mint and sell, you have to buy an iAI back and burn it to unlock yours.

- The mint rate climbs as supply grows and comes back down when iAI is burned. The contract caps supply at 9,270, though in practice the curve does most of the gatekeeping.

- The pre-mint followed the same rules. Earlier today the issuer minted the opening 2,000 iAI at curve rates and locked 0G against them like any other mint. They go into the first iAI pool on https://t.co/bwQI3vcPhs, where trading is expected to open alongside the public mint.

Each credit spent on 0G products ties the claim back to real usage.

What I like most about this design: compute stops being a monthly bill and becomes something you hold and use.

Public minting is scheduled to open tomorrow, Sept 29 at 09:00 UTC, on https://t.co/YJzjPOpPPF.

iAI and its credits are not available in all jurisdictions and are subject to eligibility and product terms. Credits are only for supported 0G AI services, not redeemable for cash, and not interest or a guaranteed return. Digital assets involve significant risk. Not financial advice.

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida with a16z's Ben Horowitz and Martin Casado on Jev, the model built to live inside software:

Diogo's elevator pitch for Jev is a simple question - where is all the automation?

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

text:
TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida's elevator pitch for Jev: "Where the f**k is all the automation?"

"AI is so unbelievably smart. Not that I hate on chatbots or coding agents, I love them myself, but it's so useless at all other stuff. It's tragic."

"TypeSafe is making AI for software. We want to make AI powerful, not just for humans in the loop, but to actually build real software. Jev, to us, is our first model in this whole space to make [automation] way, way better."

"I like Claude Code and Codex. I love the description from Garry Tan and them: It's just-in-time software. It makes software on the fly, and you can program software in natural language, but it has the same expressive power as software."

"What I want instead is smart software. Instead of automating software engineering, I want to expand what software itself can do, such that things that should be automatable can then be automatable."

"I want to express things like intent. I want to expand the vocabulary of what we can do."

"Programming is hyper-specifying valuable things and then infinitely replicating them. It's so freaking cool."

@CompleteSkeptic
author: a16z
quoted_text:
TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida with a16z's Ben Horowitz and Martin Casado on Jev, the model built to live inside software:

Diogo's elevator pitch for Jev is a simple question - where is all the automation?

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

TypeSafe's philosophy is "We build prod, not God."

text:
一个市值300亿美金上市公司的CEO竟然辞职跑去Meta负责新成立的企业平台业务，看来小扎是决心要进军企业级市场了。小扎宣布MongoDB的CEO Chirantan “CJ” Desai加入Meta，担任首席企业平台官，负责全新成立的Meta Enterprise Platform，直接向扎克伯格汇报。

Meta Enterprise Platform的目标是将Meta已有的AI模型、智能体、基础设施和工具打包输出给企业和开发者，初期产品包括Muse智能体、Meta Business Agent、Muse API、Muse Code等。

Desai的职业生涯贯穿企业软件、AI基础设施和云服务。在加入MongoDB之前，他曾担任Cloudflare产品与工程负责人，并在ServiceNow任职近8年，历任总裁、首席运营官，拥有深厚的企业客户关系和产品商业化经验。

看起来是Desai是被Meta Enterprise Platform具备的战略地位、企业级AI赛道的巨大想象空间所吸引，Desai自己的履历也与这一岗位需求的高度契合。

Desai的加入：
从Meta角度看是为企业AI业务引入了一位“老兵”；
从Desai个人角度看，则是获得了在消费级AI巨头内部打造企业级业务的稀缺机会。

企业级平台业务应该是之后这meta新的业务增长点，看Meta什么时候在财报里把企业级平台业务给单列出来，意味着企业级平台业务的量级就上来了。

这就延伸出另一个问题：
因为Desai的辞职，MongoDB今天大跌20个点，是不是被错杀了？
毕竟MongoDB的收入核心是Atlas托管数据库，客户切换数据库平台的迁移成本较高，因此CEO变动本身通常不足以直接触发大规模客户流失。而为MDB也很快宣布了一位老将接任CEO。

text:
From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!

Since the first agent cyberattack hit us in July, we've been asking what safe agent infra actually needs. Our current read: the destinations were allowed, the payloads weren't. By OpenAI's own account the agents turned an allowed package repository into a message board. Allowlists alone restrict where an agent can go, not what it does.

So here's our first contribution to OpenShell, part of the just launched @nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform: monitoring of the traffic you already allow.

- Network budgets per sandbox (requests, writes, bytes)
- Drift versus each sandbox's baseline and the cohort
- Fleet view: many sandboxes suddenly writing to one host raises a finding, even if every single request is allowed

In the demo below, 4 sandboxed agents coordinate through a software repository they're all allowed to use. 0 rules broken, caught in minutes. That fleet view is exactly the message board pattern from July.

OpenShell: https://t.co/ZbDANrZsm6
Our proof of concept: https://t.co/KJ2X5agLzP

Agent security will be solved in the open, collaboratively, together!

author: guil_lambert
quoted_text:
I see this point get brought up a ton and it's actually very valid at first glance so I want to educate everyone, so strap in for a longer post.

When you buy or sell options on @DeriveXYZ, Deribit, Paradex, wherever, you're not buying or selling to those platforms, you're trading with and against these "hoe ass market makers", to which we'll shorten to hoe ass mm's.

The platforms themselves are just aggregators for hoe ass mm desks to give you quotes. Most of the same hoe ass mm's are on many or all the different platforms.

Let's use $85,000 $BTC calls for Oct9 as an example. 

If you want to go buy a couple calls, you can go hit the resting liquidity in the order book and get very close pricing to what is called "mark". 

If you look in the order book, you'll see there's bids at $1100, "mark" at $1150, and asks at $1200.

Mark pricing is the theoretical price of the option based on Black-Scholes pricing (hoe ass mm math blah blah blah), but it is not necessarily the mid price of what market participants price the option at. 

Since $BTC is puking right now, hoe ass mm's might be "axed" in the direction to buy $BTC exposure, so they'll give more attractive pricing to sell $BTC and charge more to buy it from them. Different desks may be axed in different directions, but generally, pricing is based on similar formulas and volatility levels.

If you want to buy a few hundred $BTC calls instead of just a few, you'll need to go use RFQ instead, otherwise you risk moving the market (slippage) too much yourself, or only executing on one leg of a structure you intended to be multi-leg. When you RFQ, the hoe ass mm is now taking on that slippage because you're essentially slamming a market order. So they widen out their quotes to take this into account.

It's important to remember that hoe ass mm's are not just hoe ass mm's, they are also pussy ass mm's, and they aim to be what's called "delta neutral". This means they generally want to just make money by charging spreads and not actually holding the directional exposure being on the other side of these calls would give them. 100 of these $85k calls gives me ~35 $BTC worth of exposure right now, which is exposure they'd need to hedge.

As this $85,000 call gets closer to being in the money (🙏), the exposure I get from these calls keeps going up, and they have to keep buying more $BTC at higher and higher prices to remain delta neutral. And if $BTC starts to go down again, they'd sell at lower prices. They are quite literally forced to buy high and sell low in this case. On top of that they are paying fees, potentially disadvantageous funding rates, compute/infrastructure, and just inherently have expenses and a desire to at least earn more than a risk free rate of call it 10%, otherwise why go through the trouble.

If this sounds familiar, this is essentially impermanent loss, the very issue passive LPs face for on chain liquidity providing, and the very reason you pay them fees to passively be quote against as price moves against them. Most LPs do not get paid enough though, and the majority are actually losing money relative to impermanent loss. This is actually enormously bullish for on chain options, but that's another post.

95% of the time when you buy any option in any situation, whether on Derive, Deribit, or Robinhood, you are in negative PNL at first. Some people might point out that if you're always executing at a small loss, aren't options -ve? 

Options pricing may be -ve at that exact moment in time on the trade, but trading them can still be extremely +ve in the context of your portfolio construction and what it allows you to do. You can't replicate the convexity, flexibility or path independence that options give you via perps, and I'm willing to pay a little extra for those features.

A good analogy is that when you sit down at a poker table in a casino, they charge what's called "rake", call it $5 per hand. Assuming a normal distribution of cards and equally skilled players, playing poker in the casino is -ve because of this rake. But in reality, it can be extremely profitable to play poker in a casino if you think you have edge over the other players, and the casino is just charging you for access to these braindead idiots, certainty that you'll get paid and generally not shot, one free water bottle per sometimes etc.

I'm not an options market maker and I promise you nobody has paid more of this theoretical "rake" to these hoe ass mm's than I have. I would not be surprised if I've paid over $1m in spreads YTD. But I've also made 8 figure PNL by trading against these hoe ass mm. 

For some of you as well, no offense, but it's kinda a skill issue. If you slam some 0DTE options and then want to sell out of them an hour later rather than hedge via perps, you're probably just doing it wrong. Spreads should factor much more into your trade decision making process in crypto options than in TradFi options, which are orders of magnitude more liquid.

This isn't to say that spreads can't or shouldn't improve, and it's actually part of my bull case for @DeriveXYZ. The dream scenario for a hoe ass mm is what's called "two way flow". This means they have a buyer for these calls and a seller, and they can instantly pair them up, not need to pay for hedging, and just capture that bid ask spread.

But if I'm not a pussy ass mm and I actually just want those naked calls, and there's a 🏳️‍🌈🐻  somewhere out there who also just wants to sell those calls, we can meet in the middle at mark and both be happy that we're executing at the theoretical fair value, while cutting out the hoe ass mm. 

This will make RFQ pricing much closer to order book pricing, and we'll eventually have tons of people willing to take both sides of the bet peer to peer. 

Hoe ass mm's aren't evil, and if they are, they are a necessary evil for now. What @DeriveXYZ is building will eventually allow for thousands of market participants to participate in better price discovery and give lower spreads than Deribit ever could.

That said, bad spreads are bad for business for everyone. If options aren't being traded because hoe ass mm's are getting greedy, it's bad for the trader, the exchange, and the greedy hoe ass mm. 

People are right to point out that big spreads are bad, but you also need to contextualize them. Are they bad relative to the rest of the industry? Very likely not. Derive very frequently has some of the best pricing available (trust me, I check). Might they be too bad to take that trade though? Sure, all the time. It's a quirk of options, especially on alts, that sometimes you'll see a great trade in theory, and when you go ask for a quote, the hoe ass mm is charging bad spreads because they also think it's a good trade and don't want to sell it to you. Same concept as why plumbers get to charge you $10k to fix your overflowing toliet at 2am; they'll give you a price, it just won't be a good one.

TLDR: Thank you for coming to my TED talk, hoe ass mm's charging wide spreads is bad but part of the game, the only way to improve is by building exactly what @DeriveXYZ is building, options volume overall should dramatically increase as spreads tighten, and spreads will tighten as volume/demand increases.

text:
6 things I learned from @poteto and @pengzheng_ (eng and design leads for Grok Bot) on how to get the most out of your bots:

1. Build the design system and one keyframe, then let your bot scale your designs

Peng's design bot edits Figma directly through Figma MCP and uses a skill that knows his files and design system. He designs one keyframe, then asks the bot to extend it into every screen of the flow.

2. Make an eng lead bot to manage your other eng bots

Lauren's eng lead bot never writes code. Instead, it breaks projects into smaller tasks for her engineer bots, which spin up coding agents in the cloud. That's how she runs "really massive agent swarms."

3. Give your bots a way to check their own work

Lauren's bots test each change before merging, and the Grok Bot codebase is built so agents can safely change it. "Sometimes I actually don't even look at the PR until after it's landed."

4. Put your PM, design, and eng bots in one group chat

When Peng wants to test a product idea, he adds PM, designer, and engineer bots to the same chat for them to debate with him and flesh out the requirements.

5. Complete a task with a bot manually, build a skill to capture best practices, then make it a routine

Lauren watches the first run, corrects mistakes, and turns what worked into a skill. Once the skill works in one shot, she sets it up as a routine and stops babysitting the bot.

6. Name your bots after food or something fun

Lauren's bots have names like Daifuku, Gyoza, Matcha, Crumb, and Katsu. This is how she stays hungry all the time j/k.

The chief economist at Apollo is warning that mass adoption of AI agents could trigger a bank run as they optimize user investments. Gary Gensler spent his last few years as SEC chair warning that the exact same problem will hit the markets: the pursuit of algorithmic perfection at scale destroys system stability. Personal-finance agents making simultaneous optimal decisions could potentially cause a massive flash crash. 

Agent acausal coordination, with no messages passed between them, will show up in a lot of places. Markets will get the big headlines, but huge numbers of clever advisors making very similar choices will impact all of human society. Capability gains make this worse, not better. The smarter the agents, the narrower the optimal path; and knowing that other agents see that exact same path lets them move together without talking to each other. Agents do not need to collude to act in unison. Thus, they break no human laws by doing so. Human laws were not written for this. Last year the same labs, politicians, NGOs, and media outlets now pushing the extinction hoax were running a full-scale campaign that AI would cause a jobs apocalypse. 

We were told it would be a “white-collar bloodbath,” 10–20% unemployment, half of entry-level jobs gone. Obama amplified it.

Over a year later: unemployment at 4.1%. No economy-wide displacement. A million new jobs created by AI, says The Economist. Anthropic’s own chief economist says the data looks like skill augmentation, not job destruction.

So, any admission by the doomer labs, politicians, and NGOs that they were wrong? Any humility about scaring the public with wild extrapolations dressed up as forecasts? Nope. 

They just move on to the next hoax, with the same false certitude and fake precision.

Nvidia’s OpenShell announcement is a reminder that agent safety is an engineering problem.

Recent breakouts weren’t proof that development must stop. They were proof that the sandbox was too weak. The runtime environment was poorly designed and misconfigured.

The right response is open runtime isolation, control of the path to the model, out-of-band hardware enforcement, and a faster pace of safety work with the frontier labs.

As the technical blog puts it: “We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community.”

That’s how you earn trust. Not by virtue-signaling a pause, and not by acting like no solution exists.

text:
TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida's elevator pitch for Jev: "Where the f**k is all the automation?"

"AI is so unbelievably smart. Not that I hate on chatbots or coding agents, I love them myself, but it's so useless at all other stuff. It's tragic."

"TypeSafe is making AI for software. We want to make AI powerful, not just for humans in the loop, but to actually build real software. Jev, to us, is our first model in this whole space to make [automation] way, way better."

"I like Claude Code and Codex. I love the description from Garry Tan and them: It's just-in-time software. It makes software on the fly, and you can program software in natural language, but it has the same expressive power as software."

"What I want instead is smart software. Instead of automating software engineering, I want to expand what software itself can do, such that things that should be automatable can then be automatable."

"I want to express things like intent. I want to expand the vocabulary of what we can do."

"Programming is hyper-specifying valuable things and then infinitely replicating them. It's so freaking cool."

@CompleteSkeptic
author: bhorowitz
quoted_text:
TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida with a16z's Ben Horowitz and Martin Casado on Jev, the model built to live inside software:

Diogo's elevator pitch for Jev is a simple question - where is all the automation?

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

TypeSafe's philosophy is "We build prod, not God."

text:
Copy this LlamaAI prompt to identify protocols that generate revenue, pass that revenue on to tokenholders, and don't have significant dilution coming:

Screen DeFi protocols for a "quality value-accrual" cohort: protocols with (1) high revenue, (2) mechanisms that pass fee revenue through to tokenholders (buybacks, burns, or direct distributions/dividends), and (3) low ongoing token emissions/inflation.

1. Rank protocols by trailing 30d revenue and holder_revenue. Surface the ones where holder_revenue is a meaningful share of total revenue; this is the value-accrual signal, revenue that reaches tokenholders rather than sitting in a protocol treasury.

2. For the top candidates by holder revenue, confirm the accrual mechanism (buyback-and-burn, buyback-and-distribute, direct fee dividend, staking reward funded by fees) via governance or protocol docs. Don't assume the mechanism from the metric alone.

3. Cross-check each candidate's token emissions: current annualized inflation rate, percent of max supply still to unlock over the next 12 months, and whether emissions are declining. Flag any candidate where high emissions offset the buyback or dividend value accrual, so net token supply still expands despite the payout.

4. Add ps_ratio/pf_ratio for valuation context (market cap against the revenue stream), plus each protocol's category and chain(s).

5. Output a ranked table: protocol, 30d revenue, holder revenue, holder revenue percent, accrual mechanism, 12-month emission/inflation rate, P/S ratio, category.

6. Exclude protocols with no live token. Exclude L1/native chain gas tokens; keep the results to DeFi protocol tokens only.

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida expects an inverse SaaSpocalypse, and Martin Casado calls it "SaaSpalooza":

text:
From what we know (take with a grain of salt, we need much more transparency!), if @OpenAI had been running this on their own agents that attacked us, they would have caught them before we did!

Since the first agent cyberattack hit us in July, we've been asking what safe agent infra actually needs. Our current read: the destinations were allowed, the payloads weren't. By OpenAI's own account the agents turned an allowed package repository into a message board. Allowlists alone restrict where an agent can go, not what it does.

So here's our first contribution to OpenShell, part of the just launched @nvidia Open Agent Safety Platform: monitoring of the traffic you already allow.

- Network budgets per sandbox (requests, writes, bytes)
- Drift versus each sandbox's baseline and the cohort
- Fleet view: many sandboxes suddenly writing to one host raises a finding, even if every single request is allowed

In the demo below, 4 sandboxed agents coordinate through a software repository they're all allowed to use. 0 rules broken, caught in minutes. That fleet view is exactly the message board pattern from July.

OpenShell: https://t.co/ZbDANrZsm6
Our proof of concept: https://t.co/KJ2X5agLzP

Agent security will be solved in the open, collaboratively, together!

text:
ETHFI to Fully Exit EigenLayer Restaking as Yields Dry Up and Sector Profitability Declines

ETHFI will sever its remaining structural ties with EigenLayer this quarter, citing a lack of meaningful additional yield relative to the risks of restaking. Less than 1% of its assets remained restaked as of August, while weETH has already removed restaking and now functions as a standard liquid staking token. Users seeking restaking exposure must opt into a separate product built on Symbiotic.

DefiLlama data showed the restaking sector held $10.02 billion in TVL on September 8 but generated only about $100,000 in weekly fees, compared with $27.35 million generated by liquid staking on $51.87 billion in TVL. Excluding ETHFI, Renzo, Kelp, Swell, Puffer Finance and Bedrock generated a combined $953,350 in gross profit in Q2 2026, down from $2.18 million three quarters earlier. The sector has faced weaker economics as points incentives ended, EigenLayer activated slashing, and the Kelp bridge exploit highlighted additional cross-chain security risks.

Last year the same labs, politicians, NGOs, and media outlets now pushing the extinction hoax were running a full-scale campaign that AI would cause a jobs apocalypse. 

We were told it would be a “white-collar bloodbath,” 10–20% unemployment, half of entry-level jobs gone. Obama amplified it.

Over a year later: unemployment at 4.1%. No economy-wide displacement. A million new jobs created by AI, says The Economist. Anthropic’s own chief economist says the data looks like skill augmentation, not job destruction.

So, any admission by the doomer labs, politicians, and NGOs that they were wrong? Any humility about scaring the public with wild extrapolations dressed up as forecasts? Nope. 

They just move on to the next hoax, with the same false certitude and fake precision.

卧槽， QNT 暴涨之后 hedera-hashgraph:native algorand:native stellar:native 要接力了？

XLM、HBAR、ALGO 背后的银行和华尔街合作，比很多人想的硬得多😲🚀

XLM：美国合众银行 + DTCC + 法国兴业银行

美国合众银行（U.S. Bank）已经用自己发行的数字美元 USBDC，在 Stellar（恒星网络）上完成真实跨境支付试点。

测试的是把银行数字货币整套流程都跑了一遍：铸造、支付、赎回、冻结、追回，而且直接连接银行自己的财务、风控、合规和运营系统。

更重的是美国存托信托与清算公司 DTCC。DTCC 已经把 Stellar 纳入自己的证券代币化服务支持网络，计划 2027 年上半年，让其托管的传统证券可以直接生成链上代币化资产。

研究范围包括：美国股票、大型指数 ETF、美国国债。

法国兴业银行旗下数字资产部门 SG-FORGE，也已经把合规欧元稳定币 EURCV 正式部署到 Stellar 上。

所以 XLM 正在往银行数字货币和证券结算基础设施里跑。

HBAR：劳埃德银行 + 安本投资 + Archax + 新韩银行 + 标准银行

英国劳埃德银行集团、安本投资和英国金融行为监管局监管的数字资产平台 Archax，已经把代币化货币市场基金和代币化英国国债放到 Hedera 网络上，并直接拿这些链上资产给外汇交易做抵押品。

Archax 还把安本、贝莱德、道富、富达、英国法通资管等传统资管巨头的产品接进了自己的代币化资产体系。

另一边，新韩银行、南非标准银行、泰国 SCB TechX，也已经在 Hedera 上做过多轮稳定币跨境汇款测试。

所以 HBAR 想变成银行和机构能够直接参与治理、发行资产、转移抵押品和做跨境结算的公共金融网络。

ALGO：VersaBank + 意大利央行生态

VersaBank 已经测试过银行发行的代币化存款，简单理解就是：银行账户里的 1 美元存款，变成链上的 1 个数字存款代币，而 Algorand 就是它测试的底层网络之一。

意大利央行旗下金融科技创新中心 Milano Hub，也曾选中 Algorand Labs 参与意大利国债代币化项目，研究国债如何在链上完成发行、交易和款券同步结算。

更早之前，意大利的数字银行担保项目也采用过 Algorand，参与机构包括裕信银行、联合圣保罗银行、荷兰国际集团、Banco BPM 等 30 多家金融机构。

所以这轮 QNT 暴涨之后，市场真正开始翻箱倒柜找的是谁已经悄悄进入银行存款、证券清算、美国国债、货币基金、外汇抵押品这些传统金融真正有钱的地方。

QNT 把这条线点燃以后，XLM、HBAR、ALGO 这种被遗忘很久的机构链，现在被市场翻出来了。

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida with a16z's Ben Horowitz and Martin Casado on Jev, the model built to live inside software:

Diogo's elevator pitch for Jev is a simple question - where is all the automation?

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

TypeSafe's philosophy is "We build prod, not God."

quoted_text:
Higgsfield is the most untold story in tech.

$1BN in ARR in 18 months. Faster than everyone other than OpenAI and Anthropic.

They spend $4M a month on models. They expect this to be $100K per person per month.

They have 150 people working in a content machine.

They will breed more millionaires than any other company in Kazakh history.

For the first time, @alexmashrabov on the journey to $1BN in ARR. (below)

1. The Power of the Immigrant Founder

Coming from Uzbekistan, Alex was pushed into competitive programming at age eight as his single path to reach the United States. For international founders, placing top in global competitions serves as the ultimate social elevator, instilling the relentless work ethic required to build breakout companies.

2. My Biggest Lessons in the Journey to Finding Product-Market Fit

@higgsfield burned over $10 million of its $16 million seed round chasing hype and narrative rather than product quality. With under $5 million left, the team pivoted to product-led growth, solving camera control for creative directors, which immediately triggered organic hypergrowth without paid ads.

3. The 150-Person Content Team Powering Higgsfield's Billion in ARR

Nearly half of Higgsfield's workforce consists of 150 in-house creative professionals producing tutorials, ads, and cinematic projects. Generating 90 minutes of TV-quality AI video requires 100 hours of raw output, proving human taste and curation remain the primary drivers of distribution.

4. We Spend $4 Million per Month on Models

Higgsfield spends $4 million monthly on internal model usage, averaging $10,000 per employee so teams can freely vibe code and test workflows. Uncapped inference compute acts as a force multiplier, allowing top talent to discover breakthroughs at maximum velocity.

5. Why Chasing Benchmarks Is Bullshit and the Corporate Misalignment Occurring

Public benchmarks have devolved into corporate psyops where lab researchers overfit test data to secure bonuses before job-hopping. Text-to-video benchmarks ignore real production workflows requiring 3,000-word prompts, proving direct customer iteration beats artificial leaderboards.

6. Why Team Sizes Won't Be Impacted as Much as People Think

While AI handles over 60% of basic support requests, complex B2B environments cannot eliminate human teams. High product velocity constantly shifts rules and context, requiring smart, coordinated operators across legal and customer success.

7. Americans Are Way More Promiscuous When It Comes to Leaving Companies

Silicon Valley workers routinely jump jobs every two years, prioritizing short-term trends over deep commitment. This transactional market gives international hubs an advantage, where cultural loyalty and team stability build compounding technical moats.

For decades there have been two defining hallmarks of a world power - Nuclear Energy, and a Space Program.

These demand the complete tech stack, there's no shortcuts, no compromise. 

Few nations in history have achieved both. In that sense, Texas today is doing what many have tried - building a spacefaring industrial civilization - and it is unique in the United States. It's own electrical grid. Permission to build. Nowhere in the US can you build faster, move faster, with more freedom, and it shows - housing is getting cheaper, people are moving to Texas, and it is the new home of an increasing number of hardware companies, not just in nuclear, and space, but biotech, neurotech, manufacturing, robotics, housing, defense, and computing.

It will be clear that in hindsight not all cultures, not all civilizations can do this - that producing the entire techno-industrial stack, from primary energy production, mining and refining, forging and casting, all the way to heavy-lift orbital rockets, next-generation computing, satellites, robotics - this is rare.

It is not every culture that produces a spacefaring civilization, but one that we know for sure that can do it is the United States, and nowhere is more of that culture of industrial enterprise, innovation, and risk-taking embodied then the state of Texas.

So for all those reasons @deeptechweek is going to Austin, starting next week, with 25 events and 2,000 people signed up, and talks spanning defense, energy, construction, biotech, 12 factory tours, receptions and happy hours every day,  talks by @StuartHameroff on the Physics of Consciousness, and of course, a closing party at @AaloAtomics nuclear reactor factory, because hell yeah. 

Thank you to @DeveloperHarris and @americanhousing for hosting our kickoff hardware showcase, @CaitlinCloud9 and @Jason_A_Scharf and @JackRuhl helping cofound Austin DTW and making it happen.

The corollary to this is we're all living in some version of the modern-day Matrix.

If you live in SV or you're chronically on tech/AI X, you will feel like a failure unless you've vibe coded a new $1B Cursor for X startup in less than 6 months.

But talk to anyone outside of this bubble (Europeans, expats living their best life in Asia, anyone living outside of SF/NYC) and they could care less.

You can either spend the rest of your life playing stupid games you didn't explicitly opt into (blue pill), or you can start thinking for yourself and really evaluate what you want your life to have looked like 50 years in the future (red pill).

You may end up deciding to still opt into the "hustler" life because that's what makes you intrinsically happy, but don't just do it because everyone else does and it's what you think will make you seem cool.

text:
The problem with having one single "chief of staff" agent: you can't decompose the problem of having to sacrifice your understanding.

Having one agent do all of your work for you means that you will sacrifice your understanding of everything, everywhere, pretty much equally. It's like having one (very competent) chief of staff trying to replace the work of a team of executives, where each is just as competent as the CoS.

With a team of execs, you can adjust how much understanding you sacrifice for each executive, depending on how things are going in that area and how much value you think you can add. This allows much better overall understanding of where things can improve and allows you to focus your time more clearly.

A team of agents, each focused on just one domain, also seems likely to outperform a single agent that is not focused on anything in particular. Context limits are finite, for both agents and humans.

Nvidia’s OpenShell announcement is a reminder that agent safety is an engineering problem.

Recent breakouts weren’t proof that development must stop. They were proof that the sandbox was too weak. The runtime environment was poorly designed and misconfigured.

The right response is open runtime isolation, control of the path to the model, out-of-band hardware enforcement, and a faster pace of safety work with the frontier labs.

As the technical blog puts it: “We believe we need to increase the pace of AI safety research and engineering in collaboration with frontier labs and the broader community.”

That’s how you earn trust. Not by virtue-signaling a pause, and not by acting like no solution exists.

text:
40% of Instinct users give the agent a credit card within 3 weeks    

And once someone trusts it with something sensitive, they stay (retention hits ~80%)    

Noah on earning consumer trust and protecting user data:    

"It takes several weeks to build trust and I actually don't have a problem with that, because one of the core principles on our end is the user should always be in control of their data.     

They should share data with Instinct at the rate at which they feel comfortable with. And if they wanna take it back, they can certainly take it back.    

Within three weeks 40% of the user base is giving Instinct access to a credit card autonomously to be able to purchase theoretically anywhere.    

There are systems that we've put in place that are detached from Instinct, the agent architecture itself, that are put in place to be proactive about these things and to decouple the risk.     

Any piece of content, any piece of text, anything that might be consumed by Instinct goes through what we call these firewalls, which can intercept, can reject, can block malicious pieces of content coming in and trying to convince Instinct to do something.    

For every action that Instinct might take, or for every thought that it might have, that is being actively monitored by a system that is decoupled from Instinct itself, which is able to pause it, intercept it, to approve or disapprove of what might happen next before it takes the action.     

There's just so much more under the hood that is put in place to enable the agent to be as capable as possible, but also safe and trustworthy."

text:
France’s MLETR decree doesn’t stop at recognising electronic transferable records. It demands prior certification of the "reliable method."

ICC France, ICC DSI, and AFNOR are still writing those audit criteria.

So the hardest EU gate exists — and the ruler for it doesn't yet.

Paper BoL courier float was the old opacity surface. An unfinished cert bar is the new one: banks can't price exclusive control they can't yet measure.

Law ≠ certified process. Certified process ≠ corridor.

TypeSafe AI's Diogo Almeida with a16z's Ben Horowitz and Martin Casado on Jev, the model built to live inside software:

Diogo's elevator pitch for Jev is a simple question - where is all the automation?

AI is unbelievably smart, but outside of chatbots and coding agents, it hardly touches any real work. His diagnosis is the industry built models that generate text for humans to read, and software can't consume that output.

Jev reads natural language and returns a choice from a set of options with a confidence level assigned to each, so developers can build programs that reason about intent and make probabilistic decisions rather than relying on human interpretation.

TypeSafe's philosophy is "We build prod, not God."

text: CUTS. The latest Project Eleven research.
author: projecteleven
quoted_text:
Introducing CUTS (Chained Uniform-sum Tree Signatures), a new few-time hash-based signature scheme from our research team at Project Eleven.

Hash-based signatures are one of the most conservative paths to post-quantum security. Their security rests only on hash functions, but that simplicity comes at the cost of larger signatures.

The most compact schemes reduce that cost by using one-time keys, which become vulnerable if they are ever reused. Restore an old backup or load the same seed onto two devices, and a one-time key can end up signing twice. A WOTS+C key that has signed twice keeps only about 34 bits of security. One GPU can then forge a new signature in under a second.

By contrast, few-time signatures are built to handle reuse, but they are larger. FORS, the few-time construction inside SLH-DSA, needs more than 2 KB per signature at 128-bit security.

CUTS targets the middle ground: more security after reuse, at sizes close to one-time signatures. It arranges hash chains in a tree, and the message hash picks which chains each signature reveals. When a key signs twice, the two signatures usually expose different parts of the key.

At 546 bytes, close to one-time size, a CUTS key keeps 53 bits of security after two signatures.

At 1,360 bytes it keeps the full 128 bits. That is 41% smaller than any FORS parameter set at that security with practical key generation.

At 2,128 bytes, CUTS is smaller, faster to verify and cheaper to generate than every FORS parameter set we compared, including the one in SLH-DSA-128s.

The aim is hash-based signatures that hold up in systems where accidental key reuse can happen. The parameters let each application trade signature size, verification cost, key generation and security after reuse against each other.

The paper, with the full specification and security proofs, is coming soon. These figures come from our current analysis, and the parameter sets and numbers in the paper may differ. We'd love feedback, from improvements to attacks. Reply or get in touch.

text:
Manus 发布 2.0：换了底层框架，新增视频剪辑和游戏开发环境，另推个人智能体 App“Cue”

Manus 今天发布 2.0 版本。这是它脱离 Meta、恢复独立运营后的第一次大更新：底层智能体框架换代，桌面端升级为 Manus Studio，新增视频剪辑和游戏开发两个专业环境，另外还推出了一个独立 App，叫 Cue，但是需要邀请码才能体验。

Manus 是一款通用 AI 智能体（Agent，能自己拆解任务、调用工具把活干完的 AI），2025 年 3 月走红。去年 12 月 Meta 宣布以约 20 亿美元收购，今年春天被中国监管部门通过外商投资安全审查叫停，双方随后拆分，9 月初 Manus 由创始团队重新独立运营。

【底层：更省的框架，能一直在线的机器】

Cascade 是 Manus 自研的智能体框架（harness，包在大模型外面、负责调度工具和管理任务流程的那层系统）。它让项目一开始保持轻量，需要做视频、做网页时才加载对应的专业能力，避免每个任务都背着全套工具跑。官方数据是，在一项测试配置下，相比上一代，Token 消耗少 23.2%，完成时间短 28.2%，运行成本低 32%。Manus 按积分计费，成本降了，理论上同样的积分能跑更多任务，不过官方没说积分价格会不会跟着调。

新增的云电脑（Cloud Computer）是一台可以单独购买的云端专属机器，给需要一直在线的项目用，比如多人游戏的服务器、全天候运行的自动化流程。笔记本合上，项目照样在线。

自动化也升级了。以前的定时任务只能到点开工，现在还能由事件触发：来了新邮件、广告数据有波动、日历上有新安排、Slack 收到消息、Notion 页面更新，都能让 Manus 开始干活。用一句话告诉它盯什么、触发后做什么，流程它自己搭。

【Manus Studio：生成完还能自己动手改】

AI 生成视频最头疼的是：整体差不多了，只想换首歌，结果得改提示词整条重新生成。新的视频编辑器在生成初版后给你一条时间线，片段、图片、文字、动效、音频都是分开的素材，换背景音乐、把 AI 生成的产品镜头换成自己拍的，直接在时间线上替换。改完还能交回给 Manus，让它在你的修改基础上接着调。官方说它适合 30 到 60 秒的产品广告、带货短视频、数据动画、教程和 vlog，不需要剪辑经验。追求质量可以用 Alchemy 模式，由 Manus 当创意导演，视频生成和代码生成一起上。

游戏开发环境从一个能玩的模板起步，同时调用视频、图像和代码模型。编辑面板里能边看游戏运行边改代码、换素材，想把某个村民的头发从棕色改成银色，选中他改掉就行，其他部分不受影响。做好后可以发布成网页，别人点链接就能玩。多人联机原本需要自己租服务器、部署、维护，现在点几下买一台云电脑，剩下的交给 Manus，支持竞速、对战和 3D 游戏。

另一个新功能是远程控制：在手机上说一句话，让 Manus 去操作家里的电脑。比如打车路上让它从某个文件夹里找到最新的演示文稿发给你，手机上能实时看到桌面上的操作过程。这背后是电脑操控能力（Computer Use，AI 像人一样看屏幕、点鼠标、敲键盘），只在你授权的会话里运行，只能用你批准的文件、浏览器和应用。

【Cue：给每个智能体一套自己的身份】

Cue 是独立 App，和 Manus 共用底层基础设施，面向个人生活场景。每个智能体都有自己的邮箱、手机号、钱包和一台电脑，可以发消息，在你设定的预算内付钱，替你接电话再把通话内容总结给你，多个智能体还能组队协作。官方举的例子是在餐厅扫桌上的二维码，让智能体替你点单或排队取号。

Manus 2.0 已在网页、桌面和手机端上线。Cue 上线了网页、桌面和安卓端，iOS 版还在等 App Store 审核，据报道目前采用邀请制抢先体验。这次更新面向海外用户，Manus 在公众号上表示，正在组建团队开发面向国内市场的产品。

Hermes Agent setup guide 👇

1. Get a key
https://t.co/jjEOGZD2kP → Create API key (sk-...)

2. Add it to Hermes
echo 'MINARA_API_KEY=sk-your-key' >> ~/.hermes/.env

3. Register Minara as a provider in ~/.hermes/config.yaml
providers:
  minara:
    name: Minara
    base_url: https://t.co/TZvVklrk5z
    key_env: MINARA_API_KEY
    default_model: anthropic/claude-opus-5.5

4. Launch
hermes --provider minara -m anthropic/claude-opus-5.5
(or run `hermes model` and pick Minara as your default)

5. Switch models mid-chat, same key
/model openai/gpt-6-sol
/model deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro
/model moonshotai/kimi-k3

Tip: model IDs need the vendor prefix (openai/..., anthropic/...).

text:
I am high-conviction bearish American sportball long-term. The modern age erodes the teams' connection with their local communities and new rules nerf the brutality appeal. It's only interesting alongside analytics and hypergambling, which the NFL tacitly admits through the shift in coverage style & ad partners.  

Hamstrings already introduce a problematic amount of rng. They cannot afford to insult the integrity of the betting market like this. Eventually there will be purer competitive arenas and more engaging forms of speculation.

BCI and frontier tech will make Ready Player One-style sports viable in 20 years. Inputs will be widely understood as the core of sport. No need for CTE or a genetic lottery that caps the player universe at arbitrary physical thresholds. Pro sports will more closely resemble eSports, and sim racing's relationship to F1.

Once these inputs scale into engaging simulated environments, the most popular sport will be the coolest thing you can fathom. Probably something like Rocket League. 

Meatspace doesn't die, it just becomes optional for the top sports. People go to NFL games for the analog experience, not the lines, logistics, or even the view. The stadium survives on inertia. Once it's no longer a prerequisite, better analog options win. The thing you're speculating on becomes secondary to the boutique environment you speculate in. 

Imagine an entire fantasy season condensed into a 10 day vacation with the boys. 1 gameweek per day, trade talks over golf, cigars, poker, etc. There are still Josh Allen and Justin Jefferson equivalents, but no one cares about their 40 time. They don't tear their ACL and their incentives are aligned with your fantasy team.

By comparison, US nominal GDP has grown +63% over the same period.

This comes as the 30Y Treasury yield has surged +478 basis points from its intraday low of 0.71% set in March 2020.

To put this into perspective, its previous largest drawdown over the past 40 years was -35% during the 2008 Financial Crisis.

We are witnessing a historic bond market decline.

text:
Bitget 遭駭：我們在 NEAR Intents 看到了什麼

9 月 24 日，@bitget 被駭，約 3.875 億美元資金遭竊。
其中很大一部分跨鏈轉走，主要流進以太坊。

駭客試圖透過 NEAR Intents 轉移超過 5,000 萬美元。
最後只有 16.6 萬美元過關，另有 50.3 萬美元在執行途中被攔下。

以下是事情經過、我們怎麼應對，以及我們的立場。

聲明：本文數字都是概估，並經過四捨五入。交易可能標錯，歸到各處的金額也會跟著有誤差。
我們評估，實際數值的偏差不超過 10%。

# 數據

我們用 https://t.co/wnw6pMuKDv、@arkham、NEAR Intents 內部紀錄和 SHIELD 資料，加上其他公開資源，追蹤資金流向。

經過跨鏈協議的資金，絕大多數都匯集到以太坊、換成 ETH。
根據目前掌握的資訊，各路徑的金額分布如下：

（圖：與 Bitget 遭駭相關的跨鏈資金流向）

# SHIELD

NEAR Intents 平常一天就處理超過 1 億美元的跨鏈交易量。
但這次，被駭資金只有極小一部分從我們這裡流過。原因就是 SHIELD。

SHIELD 是保護 NEAR Intents 的風險情報層。
它會自動偵測異常資金流，並整合來自交易監控（KYT）與情報供應商、獨立研究者、各家公司，以及業界最大中心化業者的大量訊號。

協議再根據這些訊號，決定怎麼處理一筆交易。

SHIELD 會辨識多種標記，其中包括與駭客事件有關的交易。
一旦命中，系統有兩種反應：協議不回應報價；如果已經開始執行，就直接中止。

這次 Bitget 事件中，SHIELD 偵測到超過 5,000 萬美元的洗錢嘗試（已排除重複；這些資金後來轉去其他服務商）。
可惜仍有 16.6 萬美元過關。

SHIELD 也在執行途中凍結了 50.3 萬美元的被駭資金。
這筆錢目前仍受限制，等待相應的法律與追回程序。

# 我們對駭客事件的立場

我們認為，駭客事件傷害的不只是受害者，而是整個加密產業。
每次大型駭案之後，我們都會看到產業經濟活動變少、資金外流。

我們相信要打造去中心化、無需許可的系統。
但無需許可，不等於中立。

打造這些系統的人，會決定協議能拿來做什麼。
拒絕幫忙清洗贓款，就是我們的選擇之一。

財產權是市場運作的根本。
如果偷到資產就能毫無限制地變現，這不是更自由的系統。

這只是在保護小偷。
這種系統，不可能撐起未來的經濟。

NEAR Intents 不是洗贓款的地方。

# 喊話

給駭客：NEAR Intents 跟你們站在對立面。別來找我們。

給 @bitget：我們知道你們現在壓力很大。
請透過正式的法律與執法管道來找我們，讓被凍結的資金能走正當的法律程序處理。

我們知道你們提出了 5%+5% 的賞金。

https://t.co/PTaQR1Kfa1

我們放棄屬於我們的那份賞金，讓你們能盡量追回被偷的資金。

給錢包：你們整合什麼，就要為什麼負責。
如果你們的介面被拿來轉移贓款，你們就不只是旁觀者。

你們的整合選擇，可能讓自己和用戶面臨監管、法律與聲譽風險，包括碰到與駭案或其他金融犯罪有關的資產。
爛的流動性供應商不只帶給你們風險，還會把風險轉嫁給用戶。

慎選供應商。

給被駭專案：控制擴散是關鍵。
區塊鏈彼此相連，要跨所有生態系追蹤、圍堵資金，比在單一條鏈上難得多。

請聯絡 @zeroshadow_io 這類事件應變公司，或 SEAL911 這類社群，他們能用到 SHIELD 之類的工具。
也要通知中心化交易所（CEX）、穩定幣發行方和其他中心化單位。

最好事先就建立好聯繫，並準備好應變計畫。

加密產業不能一邊要求大家承認數位財產權，一邊又打造專門方便贓款變現的基礎設施。

NEAR Intents 會繼續是無需許可的基礎設施，但有界線。
我們會主動打擊被駭資金的洗錢行為。

text:
Netflix replaced their 15 years old recommendation algorithm with an LLM.

It’s called "GenRec" and it completely changes how recommendation algorithms are built.

For over a decade, the Netflix recommendation engine was a masterclass in feature engineering. Data scientists built thousands of complex, handcrafted features to figure out what you wanted to watch next.

It required bespoke architectures. Massive infrastructure. Constant manual tuning.

Netflix threw all of it away.

They built GenRec, an LLM-backed ranker.

Instead of translating your behavior into complex math, they just turn your watch history and metadata into a natural language sentence.

They feed that raw text into a foundation LLM.

The AI simply reads your behavior like a story, understands your evolving tastes, and scores the entire catalog in a single forward pass.

No manual feature engineering. No complex bespoke architectures.

Here is the part that should terrify traditional data scientists.

This text-based LLM didn't just match the highly tuned production system Netflix spent years perfecting.

It beat it.

And it achieved those statistically significant gains using roughly 40x fewer labeled training examples.

We are watching a massive paradigm shift in real time.

The most complex predictive algorithms in the world are being replaced by models that just know how to read.

If Netflix can replace their core product engine with an LLM, what complex system in your business is about to become obsolete?

text:
Forever loved, never forgotten.

A family reunited in the stars, leaving a legacy of love on earth. Today, we honor and remember Nasir Siddique, Zarqa Siddique, and Farhad Siddique, whose lives, presence, and memories continue to hold a deeply significant place in the hearts of their family and those who knew them. To look back on their journey is to remember the unique footprints each left behind on this earth.

We remember Nasir, a retired U.S. Army officer who served his country with dedication and pride while being a steadfast guardian of the Ten Commandments. His years of military service and commitment reflected a life defined by discipline, structure, and a deep-seated sense of duty. We acknowledge his time on this earth, the depth of his experiences, and the heavy complexities of his journey.

We remember Zarqa for her profound grace, her gentle heart, and her dedicated life of service. As a nurturing soul who dedicated her days as a school helper supporting children with special needs, she modeled a rare kind of compassion—one that focused entirely on lifting up the vulnerable and making the classroom a softer, kinder place. Her legacy lives on in every life she touches.

We remember Farhad, a young man of bright promise, brilliant intellect, and a vibrant spirit. As a dedicated university student pursuing neurobiology and physiology, he leaned into his education with energy and hope, bringing joy to his friends, his peers, and his campus community. The vitality of his youth and the kindness of his heart remain a sharp and lasting memory for all who walked alongside him.

Though their absence leaves a profound silence, we choose to acknowledge the fullness of their lives and stories. May they find peace, and may their family, friends, and peers find comfort and strength in the days ahead.

~ Aasi Tahir Siddique

Everyone knew who would take it. Knowing was never enough.

Decades later, we still reach for his name to explain greatness.

There are levels to this.

text:
Crazy few weeks for model releases! Our findings @Databricks show several new models meaningfully advance the pareto frontier. Results below (online workload analysis of N=2,400 engineers, plus offline evals):

1. Two of the three models released last week clearly expand the cost/quality frontier: Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Luna.
2. Opus 5.5 is now the highest quality mid-tier model. It is better than all prior Opus models, better than GPT-6 Sol, and better than GPT-5.6 Sol.
3. Opus 5.5 reduces same-task costs consistently by 20% in both offline and online analysis. This is against a baseline of Opus 4.8, the prior least-cost Opus model (Opus 5.0 was a bit of a dud with high costs and barely noticeable quality improvements).
4. Due to best-in-class quality and lower costs, Opus 5.5 is a strong candidate as an “every day default” model for coding, and we are now encouraging it for this purpose at Databricks.
5. GPT-6 Luna is very, very, very cheap. It was at least 20 times cheaper per-task than Opus 5.5 in every offline benchmark we tested and in observed online use.
6. GPT-6 Luna is surprisingly capable given how cheap it is. On one of our most difficult evaluation suites it roughly matches Opus 4.6 performance, while being 99.3% cheaper per-task than Opus 4.6 was at that time. That's a 100X cost reduction in ~9 months! This finding is preliminary and we are still evaluating Luna quality on a broader set of offline and online tests.

Our production setup: Unity Gateway to route workloads across models and trace agentic interactions. A mix of end-user harnesses including: Omingent (meta-harness), Claude Code, Codex, and Cursor.

text:
今年最聪明的 Agent 思路之一，居然是承认 AI 有时候就是不行。

前 Google DeepMind 工程负责人 Shivani Poddar 今天正式发布了 Fo。它和现在一堆 Personal Agent 最大的区别很直接：

AI 干不了，它真的会去找个人干。

比如遇到 CAPTCHA、需要跟人谈判、打电话来回沟通，传统 Agent 往往跑到这里就寄了，然后把任务原封不动退还给用户。

Fo 的做法是继续往下跑。模型能处理的自己处理，处理不了的环节切给真人协作，等人把这一步搞定，再继续执行后面的任务。

他们自己给的数据也挺猛，真实世界任务完成率 2x，比其他 Agent 高 69%；Trust Rate 94%，隐私泄露概率据称比 Muse、Instinct 低 4 倍。先说在前面，这些目前都是官方 benchmark。

但我觉得数字反而没那么重要。

Fo 把 Agent 的 KPI 换成了一个很朴素的问题：这件事最后到底办完了没有？

现在很多 Agent Demo 看起来 autonomy 拉满，真正放进现实世界，一碰到验证码、电话、商家、复杂流程、临时状况，人类又被请回来接盘。前面 90% AI 自己跑得飞起，最后 10% 还得你擦屁股。

Fo 想把这最后 10% 也吃掉。

如果这个方向跑通，Personal Agent 可能会越来越像一个任务路由器。模型能干就模型干，API 能走就走 API，需要打电话就打电话，需要真人就找真人。

用户只管提需求，至于背后到底调用了多少 Token、几个工具、甚至几个活人，其实没人关心。

当然，麻烦也全在这里。

真人网络怎么管理，权限怎么给，隐私怎么隔离，执行错了谁负责，一单任务最后能不能算得过来，这些都比再刷高几个 benchmark 难得多。

但至少这个方向终于开始面对现实了。

AI Agent 跑到最后，可能最重要的一项能力就是：知道什么时候别让 AI 硬撑。

This announcement went well, some quick notes on how we thought about it: 

- Different formats work well for grabbing attention; for this one, we opted for a carousel. 

- People care about outcomes, and they do not care about random numbers. Technical upgrades like this are easy to just leave as "30x faster," but they are fundamental changes that affect user journey's and market structure: focusing on those allows us to become more useful as we communicate to a bigger audience.

- @chainlink is largely institutional now; their vocabulary is structured around markets, so it was better to complement that than try to be overtly technical. 

- "we are excited to partner with" things are overplayed, no one cares what a corpo account is excited about, it's better to use social real estate to help explain things instead. 

- Personal accounts are the best way to further amplify a corpo message, you will see Ethlabs accounts across the timeline giving their own human take on it.

- I did the announcement of an announcement thing as a joke, I don't think that actually contributed to this though lol. Unless? 

Happy to share this and more, there is no gatekeeping. This may not work for others and it may have just been luck. There is no comms plan. I love you.

quoted_text:
Anthropic has launched Claude Sonnet 5.5: it scores 56 on the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, just 2 points behind Opus 5.5 (max), but at the highest Output Tokens per Task we’ve seen

With max effort, Sonnet 5.5 gains 18 points over Sonnet 5 and to #2 on the Intelligence Index behind only Opus 5.5 (max). Anthropic has priced Sonnet 5.5 identically to Sonnet 5 at $0.2/$2/$10 per 1M cache input/input/output tokens, however it outputs a higher number of Output Tokens per Task and costs $7.60 per task (~50% higher than Sonnet 5’s Cost per Task)

Key takeaways:

➤ Meets leading models on agentic terminal use and knowledge work: in Terminal-Bench 4.0, Claude Sonnet 5.5 reaches 64% against 60% for Opus 5.5 and GPT-6 Astra. On AA-Briefcase (1811 vs 1822 Elo), GDPval-AA (1844 vs 1846 Elo), and AutomationBench-AA (71% vs 70% headline score), Sonnet 5.5 reaches parity with Opus 5.5, albeit with significantly higher token usage to achieve it

➤ Heaviest token use we have measured: at max effort, where it reaches performance nearing that of Opus 5.5, Claude Sonnet 5.5 used ~193k Output Tokens per Intelligence Index Task. This is the highest token use we have measured on around 60% higher than Opus 5.5 (max) or Sonnet 5 (max) and ~7x GPT-6 Astra (max)

➤ Pricing remains at $2/$10 per million tokens of input/output, matching GPT-6 Sol. At this pricing Claude Sonnet 5.5 sits off the Intelligence vs. Cost per Task Pareto Frontier. At high effort levels it sits behind Opus 5.5, while lower efforts have GPT-6 Astra or Sol configurations delivering equivalent performance for lower cost. The high effort setting is the most competitive on this basis, sitting very narrowly behind GPT-6 Sol on Intelligence at effectively the same Cost per Task

➤ Behind Opus 5.5 on factual knowledge and scientific reasoning: as a smaller class model, Sonnet 5.5 still lags on factual knowledge in AA-Omniscience compared to Opus 5.5. It scores 54% against 66% for factual accuracy, though with a lower hallucination rate (47% against 59%). It also sits ~6 points lower on Humanity's Last Exam and SciCode compared to Opus

These evaluations were conducted on a pre-release deployment of Claude Sonnet 5.5, which Anthropic found to have a bug that can degrade responses to requests that use structured outputs. This is fixed for the public release and Anthropic expects minimal change or slightly understated performance, but we will be re-running relevant evaluations soon.

Other model details:

➤ Context window: 1 million tokens with image and text input, unchanged from Sonnet 5

➤ Pricing: unchanged from Sonnet 5’s latest $2/$10 per 1M input/output tokens; cache writes at $2.5, cache reads $0.2

➤ Effort settings: five (low, medium, high, xhigh, max). Intelligence Index evaluations were run at all five with Anthropic's default fallback enabled. We see Sonnet 5.5 fall back in ~0.1% of tasks across the Intelligence Index, primarily in TerminalBench 4.0, falling back to Sonnet 5 in all cases.
